concepts.name: Fast and slow pointers with a fixed gap (Remove Nth Node From End)
LRU cache: hash map plus doubly linked list
Where an LRU cache fits in an LLM app

questions.prompt: Remove Nth Node From End in one pass: both pointers start at a dummy node before `head`. `fast` moves `n + 1` steps, then both move together until `fast` is `None`. Where is `slow`?

choices.text: On the node just before the one to remove
On the node to remove, the n-th from the end
On the list's last node, just behind `fast`
Still on the dummy node, before `head`

questions.explanation: The `n + 1` steps put exactly `n + 1` links between the pointers. When `fast` falls off the end, `slow` is `n + 1` nodes from the end, which is the node before the n-th from the end. Stopping there is what you want, because unlinking needs the predecessor: `slow.next = slow.next.next`. For `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` with `n = 2`, `slow` stops on 3 and node 4 is removed.

sources.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List - LeetCode
sources.claim: Delete the n-th node from the end and return the head, with 1 <= n <= list size; Example 1 turns [1,2,3,4,5], n = 2 into [1,2,3,5], and the follow-up asks for one pass.

questions.prompt: Why does Remove Nth Node From End need a dummy node before `head`?

choices.text: It lets the algorithm finish in a single pass instead of two
When `n` equals the length, the head goes and needs a predecessor
It stores the value of `n` for the second pointer to count down
It stops the list from turning into a cycle when a node is removed

questions.explanation: Removing a node means pointing its predecessor past it, and the head has no predecessor. With `[1, 2]` and `n = 2`, the node to remove is the head. The dummy gives it a predecessor, so the same `slow.next = slow.next.next` works, and you return `dummy.next`. The gap between pointers is what gives one pass.

sources.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List - LeetCode
sources.claim: n can equal the list size (Example 2: [1] with n = 1 gives []), so the node removed can be the head.

questions.prompt: Explain the one-pass approach to Remove Nth Node From End of List, including how you handle removing the head.

model_answer.summary: Put `fast` `n + 1` steps ahead of `slow`, both starting from a dummy node, then move both until `fast` runs off the end. `slow` is then just before the node to remove, so unlink it and return `dummy.next`.
key_points: Start both pointers at a dummy node whose `next` is `head`
Advance `fast` `n + 1` steps so the gap between the pointers is fixed
Move both one step at a time until `fast` is `None`; `slow` is now the predecessor of the target
The dummy makes removing the head work like any other node; O(length) time, O(1) space

questions.explanation: The same fast/slow idea with a different rule finds the middle of a list (fast moves twice as fast) or detects a cycle. Here the rule is a fixed gap of `n + 1`.

questions.prompt: An O(1) LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list. Why doubly linked rather than singly linked?

choices.text: A doubly linked list keeps the keys in sorted order, which eviction needs
A singly linked list can't store a value next to each key, only the key
Unlinking a node the map finds needs its predecessor; `prev` gives it in O(1)
The hash map needs the extra pointer to chain together keys that collide

questions.explanation: On every `get` and `put` you move a node to the most recently used end, which means unlinking it from the middle. The hash map hands you the node itself; with `prev` and `next` you can unlink it in O(1). In a singly linked list you'd have to walk from the head to find the predecessor, which is O(n). The list is ordered by recency, not by key.

sources.title: LRU Cache - LeetCode
sources.claim: `get` returns the value or -1, `put` updates or inserts and evicts the least recently used key when over capacity, and both must run in O(1) average time.

questions.prompt: An LRU cache has capacity 2. You call `put(1, 1)`, `put(2, 2)`, `put(1, 10)`, `put(3, 3)`. What do `get(1)` and `get(2)` return?
questions.explanation: `put(1, 10)` updates key 1's value and makes it the most recently used, so key 2 becomes the least recently used. `put(3, 3)` pushes the cache over capacity and evicts key 2. `get(1)` returns the updated `10` and `get(2)` returns `-1`. Forgetting that an update counts as a use would evict key 1 instead.

sources.title: LRU Cache - LeetCode
sources.claim: `put` updates the value of an existing key, and when a put pushes the key count over capacity the least recently used key is evicted; `get` of a missing key returns -1.

questions.prompt: Describe the data structures inside an O(1) LRU cache, and what `get` and `put` do to them.

model_answer.summary: A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency. `get` and `put` move the touched node to the most-recent end, and `put` evicts from the least-recent end when over capacity.
key_points: A dict maps each key to its list node, giving O(1) lookup
A doubly linked list (often with sentinel head and tail nodes) orders nodes from least to most recently used
`get`: missing key returns -1; otherwise unlink the node, move it to the most-recent end and return its value
`put`: update and move an existing node, or insert a new node at the most-recent end
Over capacity: remove the node at the least-recent end and delete its key from the dict, which is why nodes store their key

questions.explanation: LeetCode's LRU Cache asks for `get` and `put` in O(1) average time. The map gives O(1) lookup, and the doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering and eviction.

questions.prompt: An `OrderedDict`-based LRU cache keeps the most recently used key at the end. Which call evicts the least recently used entry?

choices.text: `self.cache.popitem(last=False)`
`self.cache.popitem()`
`self.cache.move_to_end(key)`
`self.cache.popitem(last=True)`, then `move_to_end`

questions.explanation: `popitem(last=False)` removes items in FIFO order, from the front, where the least recently used key sits. Plain `popitem()` defaults to `last=True` and removes the newest entry, the one you most want to keep. `move_to_end` reorders without removing anything. The Python docs' own `TimeBoundedLRU` example evicts with `popitem(last=False)`.

sources.title: collections — Container datatypes — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: `OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)` removes pairs in FIFO order (from the front), while the default `last=True` is LIFO.

sources.title: collections — Container datatypes — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: `move_to_end(key)` moves an existing key to the right end by default, or to the front with `last=False`; the docs' `TimeBoundedLRU` recipe calls it on every hit and evicts with `popitem(last=False)`.

questions.prompt: In the `OrderedDict` LRU's `get(key)`, the key is present. What must happen before returning `self.cache[key]`?

choices.text: Nothing: reading a key moves it to the end automatically
Call `self.cache.move_to_end(key, last=False)`
Call `self.cache.move_to_end(key)`
Call `self.cache.popitem(last=False)`

questions.explanation: Looking up a key doesn't change an `OrderedDict`'s order, and neither does assigning to an existing key. You must call `move_to_end(key)`, which moves it to the right end, the most-recent end. `last=False` moves it to the front, marking it next for eviction. Popping here would evict something on a read.

questions.prompt: Give two places where an LRU cache helps in an LLM or agent app. For each, say what the cache key is, and name one kind of result you should not cache this way.

model_answer.summary: Cache work that is expensive and gives the same answer for the same input, such as embeddings and deterministic tool calls, keyed by everything that affects the result. An LRU bound keeps memory fixed by evicting what hasn't been used recently.
key_points: Embeddings: key on the embedding model plus the exact text (or its hash), so repeated chunks or queries skip the API call
Tool results: key on the tool name plus normalised arguments, for deterministic or slowly changing tools
LRU keeps memory bounded, which suits long-running servers, and works well when recent requests predict upcoming ones
Don't cache results that change or depend on time or user state, such as the current time or a live balance, or give them an expiry (like the docs' `TimeBoundedLRU`)
`functools.lru_cache` needs hashable arguments and is per process, so each worker has its own cache

questions.explanation: The `functools` docs note that an LRU cache works best when the most recent calls are the best predictors of upcoming calls, and that its size limit stops it growing without bound in long-running processes such as web servers.

sources.claim: An LRU cache works best when recent calls predict upcoming ones, its size limit keeps long-running processes such as web servers bounded, arguments must be hashable, and impure functions such as `time()` shouldn't be cached.

questions.prompt: You decorate `def embed(text: str) -> list[float]` with a bare `@functools.lru_cache`. Which statement is true?

choices.text: By default it grows without limit until the process exits
Its cache is shared by every Uvicorn worker process
It can also cache calls where `text` is a list of strings
By default it keeps at most 128 results, evicting the least recently used

questions.explanation: `lru_cache`'s default `maxsize` is 128. Only `maxsize=None` (or `@functools.cache`) makes it unbounded. The cache lives in one process's memory, so each worker has its own. The arguments are dictionary keys, so they must be hashable: calling it with a list raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.

sources.title: functools — Higher-order functions and operations on callable objects — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: `lru_cache`'s default `maxsize` is 128; `maxsize=None` makes it unbounded, and arguments must be hashable because they key a dictionary.

questions.prompt: Which result is the worst fit for a plain LRU cache in an agent?

choices.text: The embedding vector of a document chunk
The output of a `get_current_time` tool
The parsed schema of a tool's JSON definition
The token count of a fixed system prompt

questions.explanation: An LRU cache returns the stored answer for the same key until the entry is evicted, and eviction depends on use, not age. A clock tool called with no arguments would keep returning the first time it saw. Embeddings, parsed schemas and token counts of fixed text are deterministic for the same input, which is exactly what a cache wants. Time-sensitive results need an expiry, or no cache.

sources.title: functools — Higher-order functions and operations on callable objects — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: The docs say it doesn't make sense to cache impure functions such as `time()` or `random()`; the LRU cache is for reusing previously computed values.
